slides.title: SECTION 01: UNDERSTANDING AI
slides.html:
SECTION 01: UNDERSTANDING AI

What AI Is and How Language Models Work

Probabilistic text prediction vs. deterministic computation

MODULE 09 CRITICAL THINKING
A developer guide to transforming vague chat prompts into rigorous software specifications, systematic debugging protocols, safe agent execution, and empirical code verification.

Language Models Predict Tokens

An LLM calculates the mathematical probability of subsequent tokens based on patterns in training data. It does not possess intent, consciousness, or direct access to code execution unless given explicit tools.

AI Output Is a Proposal

Because LLMs generate statistically plausible completions, their answers sound confident even when wrong. Every output is an unverified proposal requiring empirical human inspection.

mental-model — verification pipeline
Question / Specification ↓ AI Interprets Context & Tokens ↓ Generates Proposal (Statistical Hypothesis) ↓ Human Developer Reviews & Doubts ↓ Verify with Evidence (Tests, Linters, Logs) ↓ Production Delivery

slides.title: SECTION 01: UNDERSTANDING AI
slides.html:
SECTION 01: UNDERSTANDING AI

Hallucinations & Failure Modes

Why AI invents APIs, packages, and syntax out of thin air

HALLUCINATIONS

What Causes Hallucination?

Hallucinations occur when the model bridges context gaps with statistical guesses. If documentation or repo constraints are omitted, it invents plausible-sounding functions, arguments, or libraries.

Generation vs. Verification

Generating code takes seconds; validating that it respects concurrency, database transaction locks, and backward compatibility requires rigorous automated tests and human review.

Key Principle: AI output is a proposal to evaluate with proof, never automatically a fact to trust blindly.
hallucination — real example
// Model suggested function: import { useDatabaseCache } from 'next/cache'; // FATAL ERROR: Module 'next/cache' has no exported // member 'useDatabaseCache'. It was hallucinated! // Real production Next.js 15 pattern: import { unstable_cache } from 'next/cache'; const getCachedUsers = unstable_cache( async () => db.select().from(users), ['users-key'], { revalidate: 60, tags: ['users'] } );

slides.title: SECTION 01: UNDERSTANDING AI
slides.html:
SECTION 01: UNDERSTANDING AI

The Verification Protocol

Evidence-based software engineering with AI assistance

VERIFICATION

The Human-in-the-Loop Contract

Never commit AI-generated code directly to production without testing. Always verify syntax, execute test suites, inspect git diffs, and confirm behavior against official specs.

The 5-Step Reality Cycle

1. Prompt -> 2. Model Interprets -> 3. Proposal Generated -> 4. Human Inspects -> 5. Evidence Verification (tests, compiler, linters, logs).

Evidence SourceWhat It ConfirmsAI Risk Avoided
tsc --noEmitType safety, API contractsHallucinated properties
pnpm testLogic, edge casesSilent regression bugs
git diffScope, unrequested editsCollateral file destruction
Server TelemetryLatency, memory, locksUnindexed query bottlenecks

slides.title: SECTION 02: WHAT IS A PROMPT?
slides.html:
SECTION 02: WHAT IS A PROMPT?

Vague Requests vs. Precise Specifications

Why 'make me a website' fails and detailed prompts succeed

SPECIFICATIONS

Vague Prompts Breed Assumptions

When a prompt lacks technology stack, architectural boundaries, or constraints, the AI guesses every variable, resulting in generic, disconnected, or unmaintainable code.

Questions vs. Actionable Tasks

Asking 'How do I do auth?' yields a generic tutorial. Prompting 'Implement NextAuth v5 session middleware matching our schema with role-based guards' yields production code.

prompt-contrast — comparison
❌ WEAK PROMPT: "Make me a website." → Generates a generic HTML/CSS landing page with lorem ipsum. ✔ PRECISE SPECIFICATION: "Build a task dashboard using Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Neon PostgreSQL. Include user authorization, Zod schema validation, optimistic UI updates, and return a clean git diff. Inspect existing db/schema.ts before coding."

slides.title: SECTION 02: WHAT IS A PROMPT?
slides.html:
SECTION 02: WHAT IS A PROMPT?

Weak vs. Strong Prompt Comparison

Deconstructing prompt quality with real engineering examples

ANATOMY

Weak Prompt: Ambiguous

'Build a task app.' Missing: Framework, database, security, state management, validation, pagination, error boundaries, styling conventions.

Result: Hallucinates random libraries, invents local storage state, ignores your database, and breaks your project design system.

Strong Prompt: Concrete Specification

'Build a task dashboard using Next.js 15 App Router, TypeScript, and Neon PostgreSQL. Enforce user authorization, Zod validation, optimistic UI updates, and return changed files.'

Result: Produces idiomatic server actions, imports your existing db client, preserves dark theme tokens, and handles error states.

slides.title: SECTION 02: WHAT IS A PROMPT?
slides.html:
SECTION 02: WHAT IS A PROMPT?

The Prompt Economy

Token budgets, signal-to-noise ratio, and prompt hygiene

EFFICIENCY

Garbage In, Garbage Out

The quality of an AI output is strictly bounded by the precision of its input. Vague requirements inevitably yield brittle architecture and phantom bugs.

Conciseness Over Bloat

Writing a strong prompt does not mean writing a 10-page novel. Provide high-signal facts, exact file paths, schemas, and non-negotiable constraints.

slides.title: SECTION 03: THE PROMPT FORMULA
slides.html:
SECTION 03: THE PROMPT FORMULA

The 7-Pillar Universal Prompt Formula

Role + Goal + Context + Requirements + Constraints + Output + Verification

FORMULA

Role & Goal

Role sets technical perspective and tone (e.g. Senior Security Auditor). Goal establishes the exact business or technical objective.

Context & Requirements

Context provides current state, files, versions, and dependencies. Requirements state the exact capabilities the solution must deliver.

formula — 7 pillars
1. ROLE: Senior Full-Stack Developer 2. GOAL: Optimize database queries on /dashboard 3. CONTEXT: Next.js 15, Neon PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM 4. REQUIREMENTS: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE, identify slow joins 5. CONSTRAINTS: Do not alter schema or delete existing data 6. OUTPUT FORMAT: Migration SQL + TypeScript diff 7. VERIFICATION: Query latency under 50ms verified by logs

slides.title: SECTION 03: THE PROMPT FORMULA
slides.html:
SECTION 03: THE PROMPT FORMULA

Constraints, Output & Verification

Guarding boundaries and defining proof of correctness

GUARDRAILS

Explicit Constraints

State what the AI must NOT do: Do not add dependencies, do not alter unrelated files, do not rewrite database schemas, do not remove backward compatibility.

Output Format & Proof

Specify format (e.g. unified diff, JSON schema, step-by-step checklist) and define the criteria required to verify that the solution genuinely works.

Why Negative Constraints Matter: Without negative constraints ("Do not..."), LLMs default to rewriting entire files, swapping libraries, or deleting unmentioned helper functions.

slides.title: SECTION 03: THE PROMPT FORMULA
slides.html:
SECTION 03: THE PROMPT FORMULA

Formula in Action: Fullstack Optimization

A production example applying all 7 prompt pillars

EXAMPLE

Structured Anatomy

Role: Senior DBA -> Goal: Optimize slow queries -> Context: PostgreSQL on Neon, Next.js App Router -> Constraints: No schema breaking changes -> Output: EXPLAIN ANALYZE + SQL index migrations.

Flexibility as a Guideline

The formula is a mental checklist, not an immutable dogma. For a 2-line bug fix, focus on Goal, Context, and Constraints; for architectural changes, use all 7.

production-prompt.txt
Act as a Senior Database Architect. Analyze the slow query on GET /api/dashboard. Context: Neon PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, table 'orders' (2M rows). Requirements: Identify missing indexes and N+1 query patterns. Constraints: Do not change database columns. Do not add packages. Output: Show EXPLAIN ANALYZE comparison and Drizzle query fix. Verification: Query execution time drops under 35ms.

slides.title: SECTION 04: CONTEXT IS EVERYTHING
slides.html:
SECTION 04: CONTEXT IS EVERYTHING

Context Density & Attention Allocation

How language models process context windows and why relevance matters

CONTEXT

The Attention Economy

Modern models have large context windows, but relevant tokens can get diluted. Flooding the prompt with 50 irrelevant files degrades reasoning performance.

High-Signal Context

Always provide: Exact package versions, database schemas, relevant route handlers, actual error stack traces, and existing conventions.

Weak Context: "My app broke with status 500. Fix it." → Zero clues. AI has to guess between 100 possible causes. High-Density Context: "In app/api/tasks/route.ts line 24, neon() throws error: 'password authentication failed for user neondb_owner'. DATABASE_URL is defined in .env.local. Verify connection string." → Pinpoints the root cause in 5 seconds.

slides.title: SECTION 04: CONTEXT IS EVERYTHING
slides.html:
SECTION 04: CONTEXT IS EVERYTHING

Context Pyramid: What to Include

Structuring contextual information from foundation to incident

PYRAMID

Foundation & Architecture

Tier 1: Tech stack, project type, runtime. Tier 2: File structure, shared types, ORM schema. Tier 3: Directly affected functions and dependencies.

Incident Telemetry

Tier 4: Observed behavior vs expected behavior. Tier 5: Raw logs, browser console output, HTTP status codes, and reproduction steps.

TierContext ElementExample Value
1Framework / RuntimeNext.js 15.1, Node.js 20.x, Linux
2Database / ORMPostgreSQL 16 on Neon, Drizzle ORM
3Target Fileapp/dashboard/actions.ts
4TelemetryHTTP 500, error code 23505

slides.title: SECTION 04: CONTEXT IS EVERYTHING
slides.html:
SECTION 04: CONTEXT IS EVERYTHING

The Minimal Sufficient Context Rule

Maximizing model intelligence while eliminating noise

PRECISION

Avoid Premature Bloat

Do not paste your entire `package-lock.json` or entire build output. Extract the first fatal error, the relevant dependency versions, and the target file snippet.

Verifiable Ground Truth

Always tell the model which files are verified ground truth and which are user hypotheses. Instruct the model not to assume unconfirmed facts.

Rule of Thumb: Supply the smallest amount of context that adequately explains the task without requiring the model to guess your architecture.

slides.title: SECTION 05: DEFINE THE ROLE CORRECTLY
slides.html:
SECTION 05: DEFINE THE ROLE CORRECTLY

Role Priming: Framing Perspectives

Guiding the model's vocabulary, skepticism, and review standards

ROLE PRIMING

Why Roles Change Output

Setting a role primes the model's latent probability distribution toward domain-specific vocabulary, quality standards, edge-case vigilance, and tone.

Generic vs Specialized Roles

'Act as a coder' produces beginner-friendly code with tutorial comments. 'Act as a Senior Distributed Systems Engineer' focuses on idempotency, race conditions, and latency.

role-comparison
"Act as a developer" → Writes a basic fetch() function without error handling or retries. "Act as a Senior Infrastructure Engineer" → Adds exponential backoff, circuit breaking, abort signals, and structured telemetry logging.

slides.title: SECTION 05: DEFINE THE ROLE CORRECTLY
slides.html:
SECTION 05: DEFINE THE ROLE CORRECTLY

The Expert Personas Catalog

Targeted personas for distinct software engineering disciplines

PERSONAS

System & Security Personas

Senior Security Auditor (focuses on OWASP Top 10, sanitization, auth bypass), Cloud Infrastructure Architect (focuses on serverless limits, cold starts, cost).

Database & UI Personas

PostgreSQL Performance Specialist (focuses on indexes, connection pools, VACUUM), Lead Frontend Architect (focuses on accessibility, layout shifts, bundle size).

Persona NamePrimary FocusKey Output
Senior Security AuditorVulnerabilities, auth, sanitizationCWE/OWASP severity audit
PostgreSQL DBAQuery latency, locks, indexingEXPLAIN ANALYZE + SQL index
UI/UX Systems ArchitectAccessibility, token consistencyAccessible semantic HTML/Tailwind
Production QA EngineerFailing edge cases, regressionParameterized test suites

slides.title: SECTION 05: DEFINE THE ROLE CORRECTLY
slides.html:
SECTION 05: DEFINE THE ROLE CORRECTLY

Role-Playing Does Not Guarantee Accuracy

A critical boundary: Persona sets tone, not verified expertise

LIMITATIONS

The Confidence Illusion

Telling an AI to 'Act as a world-class cryptographer' does not impart mathematical superpowers; it may still generate insecure custom hashing or weak random salts.

Pair Role with Acceptance Criteria

Never rely on the role alone to enforce quality. Always combine role priming with non-negotiable technical requirements and automated test verification.

Golden Rule: Roles guide the framing and vocabulary of the response. Rigorous tests, compilers, and linters determine if the code is actually true.

slides.title: SECTION 06: REQUIREMENTS AND CONSTRAINTS
slides.html:
SECTION 06: REQUIREMENTS AND CONSTRAINTS

Requirements vs. Constraints

Defining what must be accomplished versus what must never happen

REQUIREMENTS

Functional Requirements

Requirements describe active desired behaviors: 'Add search filter by tag', 'Return JSON pagination metadata', 'Hash passwords with Argon2id'.

Protective Constraints

Constraints prevent collateral damage: 'Do not modify database schema', 'Do not introduce new npm packages', 'Preserve existing function signatures'.

slides.title: SECTION 06: REQUIREMENTS AND CONSTRAINTS
slides.html:
SECTION 06: REQUIREMENTS AND CONSTRAINTS

Guardrails for Legacy & Production Systems

Preventing accidental rewrites, breaking changes, and visual degradation

SAFETY

The Non-Destructive Injunction

AI models love to rewrite entire files from scratch. Explicitly state: 'Perform minimal surgical edits; preserve existing coding conventions and unrelated logic.'

Backward Compatibility Rules

Demand that public API contracts, database column names, and client query parameters remain 100% backward compatible unless deprecation was requested.

constraints-example
CONSTRAINTS: - Keep all border-radius strictly at 0px. - Use pnpm as the ONLY package manager; do not run npm. - Never execute git add, git commit, or git push. - Do not introduce new ORMs (stick to current Drizzle). - Keep changes unstaged for my review.

slides.title: SECTION 06: REQUIREMENTS AND CONSTRAINTS
slides.html:
SECTION 06: REQUIREMENTS AND CONSTRAINTS

Writing Strict Acceptance Criteria

The checklist that turns subjective tasks into binary passes or fails

DEFINITION OF DONE

Definition of Done

A task is only done when: 1. Existing unit tests pass. 2. TypeScript compilation passes with zero errors. 3. No secrets are logged. 4. Edge cases are handled.

Self-Review Requirement

Instruct the model: 'Before printing the final response, self-review your code against every requirement and constraint. Explicitly list any trade-offs made.'

ACCEPTANCE CHECKLIST: [ ] Task is complete ONLY when `pnpm build` succeeds with zero errors. [ ] All query parameters are sanitized against SQL injection. [ ] Empty state renders when task list length is 0. [ ] User cannot view tasks belonging to other tenant IDs.

slides.part: SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING
slides.title: SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING
slides.html:
SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING

Investigation First, Implementation Second

Why jumping straight into code generates architectural debt

INSPECT FIRST

The Premature Coding Trap

When asked to code immediately, models invent assumptions about your data models and routing, creating code that conflicts with your existing project structure.

The Read-Only Inspection Mandate

Command: 'Do not write or modify code yet. Inspect the existing repository, summarize architecture, trace data flow, and list risks first.'

1
Read-Only Audit
Zero files edited
→
2

slides.part: SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING
slides.title: SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING
slides.html:
SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING

The 8-Point Codebase Inspection Prompt

A complete framework for auditing an existing implementation

FRAMEWORK

Architecture & Data Flow

1. Current architecture & patterns. 2. File responsibilities. 3. Current feature implementation mechanics. 4. Dependencies & integrations.

Risks & Verification Strategy

5. Potential edge-case bugs & security risks. 6. Side effects of modifying files. 7. Incremental implementation steps. 8. Test verification plan.

audit-prompt-template.txt
Do not modify any files yet. Inspect the existing codebase and explain: 1. The current architecture and directory responsibilities. 2. How the current feature works from input to database. 3. Dependencies and shared utility functions. 4. Potential bugs, edge cases, and security vulnerabilities. 5. Side effects on unrelated modules. 6. The safest incremental implementation plan. Support findings with file paths and line number citations.

slides.part: SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING
slides.title: SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING
slides.html:
SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING

Distinguishing Facts from Assumptions

Requiring empirical proof and file citations from the model

EVIDENCE

File Path & Line Proof

Demand that every claim cite exact filenames and line numbers: 'Support all architectural claims with file references in the current repository.'

The Unknowns Ledger

Require the model to explicitly list what it does NOT know: 'State what context is missing rather than guessing configuration or database values.'

Claim TypeUnacceptable FormAcceptable Evidence Form
Database Table"It probably has a users table"db/schema.ts:14-28 (table 'users')
Auth Status"Auth looks secure"middleware.ts:8 checks req.auth token
Missing ContextInventing port numbers"Database port not found in .env; please provide."

slides.part: SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING
slides.title: SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING
slides.html:
SECTION 07: ASK AI TO ANALYZE BEFORE CODING

The Professional Engineering Workflow

Understand -> Inspect -> Analyze -> Identify Risks -> Plan -> Implement -> Verify

WORKFLOW

The 7-Step Cadence

High-leverage developers treat AI like an eager junior engineer: assign research first, review their plan, approve the diff, and run the tests.

Massive Time Savings

Spending 2 minutes on analysis prevents 2 hours of debugging hallucinated imports, broken state synchronizations, and circular dependencies.

STAGE 1: Understand user problem & boundaries STAGE 2: Inspect existing source code files STAGE 3: Analyze constraints, versions & data flow STAGE 4: Identify edge-case bugs & breaking risks STAGE 5: Plan incremental steps (review with human) STAGE 6: Implement minimal code changes STAGE 7: Verify with linters, tests, and diff review

slides.title: SECTION 08: THINK BEFORE SOLVING
slides.html:
SECTION 08: THINK BEFORE SOLVING

Deconstructing Problems Methodically

Observation is not causation: Diagnosing before prescribing

DIAGNOSTICS

The Symptom vs Root Cause Fallacy

Symptom: 'Dashboard load time is 6 seconds.' Bad fix: Slap Redis caching on everything. Good fix: Profile queries, discover an unindexed N+1 query.

The 9 Diagnostic Questions

What is the actual problem? Expected vs observed? What evidence exists? What could cause it? What assumptions are we making? What is the smallest safe test?

Always Remember: The first apparent cause proposed by an AI is often just a symptom. Force the model to explain the causal mechanism behind the error.

slides.title: SECTION 08: THINK BEFORE SOLVING
slides.html:
SECTION 08: THINK BEFORE SOLVING

The Scientific Method in Software

Observation -> Hypothesis -> Experiment -> Verification -> Targeted Fix

SCIENTIFIC METHOD

Formulating Testable Hypotheses

A hypothesis must be falsifiable: 'If the delay is caused by missing database indexes, running EXPLAIN ANALYZE will show a Sequential Scan on orders table.'

Smallest Reversible Step

Test one variable at a time. Never change 5 configuration files, 2 libraries, and the database schema in a single debugging attempt.

1
Observe
Log exact error
→
2
Hypothesize
Testable theory
→
3
Surgical Fix
1 variable changed

slides.title: SECTION 08: THINK BEFORE SOLVING
slides.html:
SECTION 08: THINK BEFORE SOLVING

Case Study: The Slow Dashboard

Real-world walkthrough from panic to empirical resolution

CASE STUDY

Flawed Approach

Prompting 'My app is slow make it fast' leads to unnecessary server upgrades, complex caching layers, and new points of failure.

Result: Adds Redis, breaks cache invalidation, users see stale orders, database is still unindexed and slow when cache misses.

Disciplined Approach

Inspect server logs, measure query duration, check network waterfall, identify single unindexed foreign key join, apply 1-line index, verify latency dropped to 40ms.

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders(customer_id); → Query cost drops from 12450.00 to 8.42. 0 server cost added.

slides.title: SECTION 09: LOGICAL THINKING
slides.html:
SECTION 09: LOGICAL THINKING

Core Mental Models for Programmers

Deductive reasoning, first principles, and edge-case discovery

MENTAL MODELS

First Principles Thinking

Break a problem down to its fundamental truths (HTTP requests, memory allocation, TCP sockets, disk I/O) and reason upwards from there.

Deduction vs Induction

Just because authentication worked in 10 local tests does not prove it works in production under distributed session load. Verify boundaries logically.

logical-framework
OBSERVATION: API request fails with status 403. DEDUCTION: 1. Status 403 means Forbidden (client is authenticated, but lacks permission). 2. It is NOT 401 (Unauthorized / bad credentials). 3. The failure is in authorization logic or role checks. CONCLUSION: Check role permissions on user record, not password hashing!

slides.title: SECTION 09: LOGICAL THINKING
slides.html:
SECTION 09: LOGICAL THINKING

Case Analysis: 'Login Fails'

Mapping multiple potential root causes systematically

DECISION TREE

The Multi-Cause Tree

Login failure can stem from: 1. Invalid client credentials. 2. Database connection pool exhaustion. 3. Expired JWT secret. 4. CORS header mismatch. 5. Clock drift.

Eliminating by Binary Search

Check the status code: 401 = client auth error, 500 = server exception, 504 = network gateway timeout. Use telemetry to eliminate whole branches instantly.

HTTP CodeLayer of FailureEvidence to Inspect
401 UnauthorizedClient CredentialsPassword hash compare, email spelling
403 ForbiddenAccess PermissionsUser role, tenant_id guard
500 Server ErrorBackend Crash / DBServer terminal logs, Neon pool limit
504 Gateway TimeoutNetwork / UpstreamDeadlock in DB transaction

slides.title: SECTION 09: LOGICAL THINKING
slides.html:
SECTION 09: LOGICAL THINKING

Cognitive Biases When Using AI

Guarding against automation bias, anchoring, and confirmation bias

BIAS AUDIT

Automation Bias

The tendency to favor suggestions from automated systems over human critical judgment. AI eloquence often disarms developer skepticism.

Anchoring to First Answer

Do not let the model's first suggestion anchor your entire architecture. Ask for 3 distinct technical approaches with concrete tradeoffs.

Antidote to Bias: Never ask 'Is this code good?'. Ask 'Identify 3 potential security flaws and 2 race conditions in this code snippet.'

slides.title: SECTION 10: DECOMPOSE COMPLEX TASKS
slides.html:
SECTION 10: DECOMPOSE COMPLEX TASKS

The Art of Task Decomposition

Converting overwhelming monolithic epics into atomic milestones

DECOMPOSITION

Monolithic Prompts Fail

'Build a complete multi-tenant SaaS accounting system' will produce incomplete mockups, truncated functions, and non-functional placeholders.

The Atomic Chunk Rule

Every task assigned to an AI should have a single, verifiable deliverable that can be compiled, tested, and reviewed in under 10 minutes.

MONOLITHIC PROMPT: "Create a complete e-commerce store with Stripe, database, admin panel, email notifications, reviews, inventory, and discounts." → Output truncated, incomplete functions, broken schemas. DECOMPOSED PROMPT: "Phase 1: Define Drizzle schema for products, orders, and order_items. Include foreign keys, UUID primary keys, and indexes. Do not write UI yet." → Flawless schema delivered in seconds.

slides.title: SECTION 10: DECOMPOSE COMPLEX TASKS
slides.html:
SECTION 10: DECOMPOSE COMPLEX TASKS

Deconstruction Case: Enterprise POS System

Breaking an 11-module retail system into ordered dependencies

DEPENDENCY TREE

Dependency Ordering

Layer 1: Database schemas & migrations -> Layer 2: Auth & RBAC -> Layer 3: Inventory data layer -> Layer 4: Order processing -> Layer 5: UI & Reporting.

Why Order Matters

Building UI checkout buttons before defining transaction lock mechanisms or inventory concurrency constraints guarantees extensive refactoring.

POS SYSTEM DECOMPOSITION: ├── 01_DATABASE: Schemas, foreign keys, indexes ├── 02_AUTH: Cashier vs Manager RBAC permissions ├── 03_INVENTORY: Stock deduction & optimistic locking ├── 04_CHECKOUT: Stripe / Cash transaction handling ├── 05_RECEIPTS: PDF generation & audit log └── 06_UI: Responsive cashier dashboard

slides.title: SECTION 10: DECOMPOSE COMPLEX TASKS
slides.html:
SECTION 10: DECOMPOSE COMPLEX TASKS

Sub-Task Prompting Workflow

Maintaining momentum and architectural consistency across sessions

MOMENTUM

Contract-First Sub-Tasking

Step 1: Define TypeScript interfaces and schemas. Step 2: Implement server-side CRUD. Step 3: Implement client components. Step 4: Write tests.

Context Preservation

Carry forward the schema contracts and conventions from previous steps so the AI builds each sub-module to fit the established architecture perfectly.

Session Strategy: Once a sub-task is completed and tests pass, commit it locally. Start the next prompt with a clean working tree and reference the newly committed file paths.

slides.title: SECTION 11: PLANNING BEFORE IMPLEMENTATION
slides.html:
SECTION 11: PLANNING BEFORE IMPLEMENTATION

Generating Incremental Implementation Plans

Why code execution must be gated behind written architectural approval

PLAN FIRST

The Plan-First Protocol

Instruct AI: 'Create an incremental implementation plan with objectives, files to edit, risks, and verification steps. Do not modify files until approved.'

Catching Blunders Early

Reviewing a 10-line bulleted plan takes 30 seconds and reveals flawed assumptions before a single file or database table is touched.

PROMPT TO REQUEST A PLAN: "Based on your codebase analysis, create an incremental implementation plan. For every step, specify: - Objective - Target files to create or modify - Breaking change risks - Verification command (test/lint) Do NOT implement yet. Wait for my approval."

slides.title: SECTION 11: PLANNING BEFORE IMPLEMENTATION
slides.html:
SECTION 11: PLANNING BEFORE IMPLEMENTATION

Anatomy of an Actionable Plan

Step, files, dependencies, rollback strategy, and acceptance tests

PLAN STRUCTURE

Every Step Must Be Atomic

Each step lists: Target files, exact changes, potential breaking changes, migration commands, and automated test commands.

Rollback Readiness

If step 3 fails, what is the undo plan? Plans must account for partial failures, especially in database migrations and production deployments.

Plan SectionRequirementPurpose
Objective1 sentence scopePrevents scope creep
Files ModifiedExact repo pathsPrevents collateral churn
Rollback PlanCommand to undoLimits blast radius
VerificationPass/Fail commandObjective acceptance

slides.title: SECTION 11: PLANNING BEFORE IMPLEMENTATION
slides.html:
SECTION 11: PLANNING BEFORE IMPLEMENTATION

When to Plan vs. When to Code Directly

Balancing engineering rigour with rapid development velocity

VELOCITY

Always Plan For:

Auth flows, payment integrations, schema migrations, public API changes, major refactors, multi-file features, and production deployments.

Direct Code For:

Isolated pure utility functions, localized CSS tweaks, adding a single button icon, regex validation helpers, and standalone unit tests.

slides.title: SECTION 12: PROMPTING FOR CODE GENERATION
slides.html:
SECTION 12: PROMPTING FOR CODE GENERATION

Precision Code Generation

Getting clean, production-grade, framework-idiomatic code

CODE GEN

Convention Enforcement

Specify: 'Match existing naming conventions, use strict TypeScript types, return early, avoid any, and keep functions small and focused.'

Input Validation & Boundaries

Explicitly demand validation: 'Validate all external input using Zod schemas; handle null, undefined, and empty array edge cases cleanly.'

// Clean, early-return, strictly-typed production action: export async function updateTask(rawInput: unknown) { const parsed = updateTaskSchema.safeParse(rawInput); if (!parsed.success) { return { error: 'Invalid input', issues: parsed.error.issues }; } const session = await auth(); if (!session?.user?.id) return { error: 'Unauthorized' }; return await db.update(tasks) .set({ title: parsed.data.title }) .where(and(eq(tasks.id, parsed.data.id), eq(tasks.userId, session.user.id))); }

slides.title: SECTION 12: PROMPTING FOR CODE GENERATION
slides.html:
SECTION 12: PROMPTING FOR CODE GENERATION

Preventing Anti-Patterns & Bloat

Eliminating hallucinated libraries, premature abstractions, and commented noise

ANTI-BLOAT

No Phantom Libraries

Constraint: 'Use only standard library or existing dependencies in package.json. Do not install additional packages without explicit approval.'

No Useless Comments

Constraint: 'Do not add obvious comments explaining syntax. Only preserve comments that document non-obvious business logic or algorithmic nuance.'

// BAD: Bloated with obvious comments // This sets x to 5 const x = 5; // Return the result return x + 1; // GOOD: Clean, self-documenting code const MAX_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 5; return currentAttempt + 1;

slides.title: SECTION 12: PROMPTING FOR CODE GENERATION
slides.html:
SECTION 12: PROMPTING FOR CODE GENERATION

Complete Working Code Requirement

Banning placeholders, ellipses, and unhelpful TODOs

NO PLACEHOLDERS

The '// TODO' Plague

Models often truncate complex logic with '// implement rest here'. Strictly instruct: 'Provide complete, fully working code. Do not leave placeholder comments.'

Production Error States

Demand complete handling: 'Include loading skeletons, empty states, network failure recovery, and accessible user error notifications.'

Strict Injunction: "Return complete working code. If the code is long, break it across clear consecutive files rather than omitting lines with comments."

slides.title: SECTION 13: PROMPTING FOR UI DESIGN
slides.html:
SECTION 13: PROMPTING FOR UI DESIGN

UI Reproduction vs. Arbitrary Redesign

Guiding AI to match existing design systems with pixel precision

DESIGN FIDELITY

Preserving Design Consistency

AI models default to generic blue gradients and rounded pills. Constrain: 'Preserve existing dark theme tokens, zero border-radius, and font scales.'

Feeding Design Specifications

Provide exact design tokens: Background hex codes, text color variables, spacing scale (e.g. max 20px), and mobile breakpoint conventions.

EXACT UI SPECIFICATION: - Theme: Dark palette (bg: #020617, card: #0f172a, border: #1e293b) - Spacing: Never exceed 20px (use 4px, 8px, 12px, 16px, 20px) - Corners: on all elements - Text: Crisp white (#ffffff) on dark backgrounds - Buttons: Blue button text MUST be #ffffff (never black)

slides.html:
SECTION 13: PROMPTING FOR UI DESIGN

Component-Driven Prompting

Building reusable, accessible, and responsive UI components

ACCESSIBILITY

Accessibility Standards

Require ARIA attributes: 'Ensure keyboard focus visibility, appropriate roles (dialog, combobox), screen-reader labels, and color contrast compliance.'

Responsive Matrix

Instruct: 'Test and deliver layouts that adapt seamlessly from mobile (375px) to tablet (768px) and desktop (1280px) without horizontal overflow.'

Screen SizeLayout RequirementVerification
Mobile (<640px)Single column, stacked controlsNo horizontal scrollbar
Tablet (640-1024px)2-column grid, compact spacingModal widths <90vw

slides.title: SECTION 13: PROMPTING FOR UI DESIGN
slides.html:
SECTION 13: PROMPTING FOR UI DESIGN

The 4 Levels of UI Requests

Inspiration vs. Pixel Clone vs. Incremental Polish vs. Total Redesign

TAXONOMY

Know What You Are Asking For

Level 1: Inspiration (generate layout ideas). Level 2: Exact Clone (match reference markup). Level 3: Polish (fix spacing/contrast). Level 4: Redesign.

The Visual Drift Trap

If you ask AI to 'make it look better' without reference rules, it will introduce random font weights, arbitrary shadows, and inconsistent padding.

Cloning Tip: Supply the exact HTML element structure, Tailwind classes, and SVG icons. Tell the AI: "Change only the data values; do not alter CSS class strings."

slides.title: SECTION 14: DEBUGGING WITH AI
slides.html:
SECTION 14: DEBUGGING WITH AI

Structured Debugging Protocols

Extracting root causes instead of playing whack-a-mole with symptoms

DEBUGGING

The Debugging Input Payload

1. Expected behavior. 2. Observed behavior. 3. Full stack trace / server logs. 4. Minimal code snippet. 5. Reproduction steps. 6. Environment specs.

The Last-Line Error Fallacy

Pasting only the last error line ('Internal Server Error 500') leaves the AI blind. Paste the first relevant error in the call stack.

debug-template.txt
Expected: Task status updates to 'completed' on click. Observed: UI spinner spins infinitely; network tab shows 500. Logs: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'userId') at updateTask (app/actions.ts:42:18) Repro Steps: Click checkbox on any unassigned task. Environment: Next.js 15.1, Node 20.10, PostgreSQL Neon.

slides.html:
SECTION 14: DEBUGGING WITH AI

The 8-Step Debugging Cycle

Observe -> Reproduce -> Collect Evidence -> Hypothesize -> Test -> Fix -> Regression Test -> Document

CYCLE

Surgical Fixes

Demand: 'Identify the exact root cause, explain why the bug occurred, propose the smallest safe fix, and explain possible side effects on callers.'

Regression Shield

Always require a regression unit test: 'Write a test that reproduces this exact failure scenario and confirms that the fix resolves it.'

Reproduce

→
2

→

slides.title: SECTION 14: DEBUGGING WITH AI
slides.html:
SECTION 14: DEBUGGING WITH AI

Investigating Ephemeral & Race Condition Bugs

Handling asynchronous timing, database deadlocks, and memory leaks

CONCURRENCY

Concurrency & Timing

Ask: 'Analyze this async workflow for race conditions, unhandled Promise rejections, stale closure captures, or optimistic lock conflicts.'

Network & Environment Variance

Investigate differences between local dev and cloud edge runtimes (e.g. Node.js vs Edge runtime APIs, file system access, cold-start latency).

CONCURRENCY PROMPT: "Inspect this Server Action for concurrent execution hazards. What happens if two users submit the form at the exact same millisecond? Propose a database row-level lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or optimistic versioning column to guarantee idempotency."

slides.title: SECTION 15: PROMPTING FOR SECURITY AUDITS
slides.html:
SECTION 15: PROMPTING FOR SECURITY AUDITS

Evidence-Based Security Reviews

Turning models into ruthless code auditors without destructive actions

SECURITY

The Read-Only Security Mandate

Command: 'Perform a strictly read-only audit. Do not execute destructive operations. Inspect auth guards, sanitization, and database isolation.'

OWASP Top 10 Focus

Audit: Injection, Broken Auth, Sensitive Data Exposure, XML/Entity flaws, Broken Access Control, Security Misconfiguration, XSS, Insecure Deserialization.

security-audit-prompt.txt
Perform a strictly read-only security audit of app/api/. Focus on: 1. SQL injection & unescaped dynamic queries 2. Missing authentication & role authorization checks 3. Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) 4. Secret leaks in client responses Report findings by Severity (Critical/High/Med) with file lines and PoC.

slides.title: SECTION 15: PROMPTING FOR SECURITY AUDITS
slides.html:
SECTION 15: PROMPTING FOR SECURITY AUDITS

Standard Security Finding Format

Severity, Affected Path, Vulnerability, Exploit Scenario, Remediation, Verification

VULNERABILITY REPORT

Structure Every Vulnerability

Require: Severity (Critical/High/Med/Low), File & Line, Real-world attack scenario, Business impact, Exact patch diff, and Verification test.

No Fictional Security Claims

Instruct the model: 'Distinguish confirmed exploits from speculative risks. Do not declare code secure unless every branch has been verified.'

SeverityVulnerabilityRemediation
CRITICALRaw string SQL concatenationParameterized query with Drizzle/Prisma
HIGHMissing tenant_id in WHERE clauseEnforce composite unique (id, tenant_id)
MEDIUMStack trace returned in JSONWrap in try/catch; return generic error

slides.title: SECTION 15: PROMPTING FOR SECURITY AUDITS
slides.html:
SECTION 15: PROMPTING FOR SECURITY AUDITS

Multi-Tenant & Secret Isolation

Guarding against data leaks, exposed tokens, and IDOR vulnerabilities

DATA ISOLATION

Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR)

Verify: 'Ensure every database query verifies tenant_id and user_id ownership; verify users cannot view or mutate other users' records by altering URLs.'

Secret Leak Prevention

Verify that server secrets (DATABASE_URL, API tokens) are never bundled into client-side JS or logged in public telemetry.

// DANGEROUS IDOR VULNERABILITY: await db.select().from(invoices).where(eq(invoices.id, params.id)); // SECURE TENANT-ISOLATED QUERY: await db.select().from(invoices).where(and( eq(invoices.id, params.id), eq(invoices.organizationId, session.user.orgId) ));

slides.title: SECTION 16: PROMPTING FOR CODE REVIEW
slides.html:
SECTION 16: PROMPTING FOR CODE REVIEW

The Production Code Reviewer Persona

Reviewing for correctness, safety, and performance rather than stylistic bike-shedding

CODE REVIEW

Reviewer Priorities Hierarchy

1. Correctness & Bug Prevention. 2. Security. 3. Data Integrity. 4. Backward Compatibility. 5. Performance. 6. Maintainability. 7. Style.

Actionable Findings First

Command: 'Report critical bugs and functional defects first. Do not waste space recommending variable renames or personal formatting preferences.'

PriorityFocus AreaReview Question
1CorrectnessDoes it satisfy the acceptance criteria?
2SecurityDoes it sanitize inputs and check permissions?
3Data IntegrityCan concurrent requests cause data corruption?
4CompatibilityWill existing mobile/web clients break?

slides.title: SECTION 16: PROMPTING FOR CODE REVIEW
slides.html:
SECTION 16: PROMPTING FOR CODE REVIEW

Reviewing Diffs Effectively

Feeding Git diffs to AI for surgical pre-commit audits

GIT DIFF

The Git Diff Prompt

Pass `git diff` into the prompt: 'Analyze this uncommitted diff. Identify any regressions, unintended edits, console logs, or security risks introduced.'

Scope Verification

Confirm that only files relevant to the task were modified. Flag any collateral edits to config files or unrelated modules.

DIFF AUDIT PROMPT: "Review this git diff before I commit: `git diff` Answer: 1. Did I accidentally leave any debug console.log or test tokens? 2. Are any modified files outside the scope of adding user avatars? 3. Are there any edge-case null pointer exceptions in the diff lines?"

slides.title: SECTION 16: PROMPTING FOR CODE REVIEW
slides.html:
SECTION 16: PROMPTING FOR CODE REVIEW

Code Review vs. Code Rewriting

Preserving project architecture and preventing unauthorized refactoring

PRESERVATION

Respecting the Author's Architecture

A reviewer assesses whether the code satisfies requirements safely within the current architecture—not whether they would have built it differently from scratch.

Constructive Remediation

Every critique must include a minimal, concrete code example demonstrating how to fix the problem safely.

Review Command: "Provide actionable comments with minimal code fixes. Do not refactor modules that are already working unless a critical vulnerability requires it."

slides.title: SECTION 17: PROMPTING FOR DATABASE CHANGES
slides.html:
SECTION 17: PROMPTING FOR DATABASE CHANGES

Database Migrations & Data Safety

Protecting schemas, tables, and production data from reckless alterations

DATA SAFETY

The Golden Database Rule

Never blindly execute AI-generated SQL migrations on production. Inspect locks, downtime impact, index rebuild times, and rollback scripts.

Safe Migration Prompting

Instruct: 'Analyze this schema change. Explain table locks, performance impact on large tables, backward compatibility, and write a reversible DOWN migration.'

HAZARDOUS AI MIGRATION: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL; → Table lock on 10M rows causes downtime! PRODUCTION-SAFE MIGRATION: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'pending'; -- Or use Expand-and-Contract with nullable column first.

slides.html:

PostgreSQL & Neon Specific Considerations

Connection pooling, serverless branching, and index optimization

NEON POSTGRES

Connection Exhaustion & PgBouncer

Serverless functions create many short-lived connections. Prompt AI to configure transaction pooler ports and avoid holding long locks.

Branch-First Verification

Use Neon instant branching to test migrations against real production data copies in an isolated sandbox branch before touching primary.

slides.title: SECTION 17: PROMPTING FOR DATABASE CHANGES
slides.html:
SECTION 17: PROMPTING FOR DATABASE CHANGES

Data Loss Prevention Checklist

Flagging DROP, TRUNCATE, ALTER TYPE, and table rewrite hazards

ZERO LOSS

Destructive Operation Warnings

Demand: 'Explicitly highlight any command that drops columns, rewrites entire tables, or truncates data. Propose zero-downtime expand-and-contract steps.'

Verification Queries

Require the model to provide verification queries: SELECT statements to confirm index usage, foreign key integrity, and row counts before and after.

VERIFICATION QUERIES TO REQUEST: -- 1. Check index validity: SELECT indexrelid::regclass, indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE indisvalid = false; -- 2. Confirm row counts match pre-migration backup: SELECT count(*) FROM orders;

slides.title: SECTION 18: USING AI CODING AGENTS
slides.html:
SECTION 18: USING AI CODING AGENTS

From Chatbots to Autonomous Coding Agents

Understanding IDE assistants, repo-aware CLI tools, and background agents

AGENTS

The Tool Spectrum

Chat AI (isolated text) -> Inline Copilots (code completion) -> Repository Agents (read files, run bash, run tests, create diffs).

Tool Access & Agency

Coding agents have tools to inspect your filesystem, run terminal commands, and modify code. Agency demands strict operational constraints.

Agent TypeCapabilitiesSafety Requirement
ChatbotGenerates markdown text onlyManual copy-paste review
Inline CopilotAutocompletes cursor tokensTab completion scrutiny
Autonomous AgentExecutes bash, edits files directlyStrict permission boundaries

slides.title: SECTION 18: USING AI CODING AGENTS
slides.html:
SECTION 18: USING AI CODING AGENTS

Agent Capabilities & Permission Boundaries

Granting enough power to solve tasks while preventing catastrophic errors

PERMISSIONS

Read vs Write vs Execute Permissions

Safe default: Allow file inspection freely, allow code editing within target directories, but require approval for destructive commands (rm, drop, git push).

Tool Awareness

Different agents have different capabilities. Do not assume an agent has internet access, database credentials, or browser automation unless verified.

Permission Matrix: Read Files = Auto-allowed. Run Read-only Bash = Auto-allowed. Run Tests = Auto-allowed. Git Commit / Push = FORBIDDEN. Deploy = FORBIDDEN.

slides.title: SECTION 18: USING AI CODING AGENTS
slides.html:
SECTION 18: USING AI CODING AGENTS

Guiding Agents with Context Files

Using AGENTS.md, rules, and customization skills to govern behavior

AGENTS.MD

System Rules & Guardrails

Define persistent repository rules: 'Never run git push. Keep all border-radius at 0. Use pnpm only. Do not add code comments.'

Repeatable Workflows

A strong rules file ensures the agent adheres to your architecture and conventions across every prompt and every session automatically.

# AGENTS.md / Repository Instructions - Package Manager: Use pnpm ONLY (never npm or yarn) - Version Control: NEVER execute git add, git commit, or git push - Styling: Zero border-radius on all elements (border-radius: 0 !important) - Clean Code: Do NOT add code comments unless explicitly requested - Output: Leave all changes unstaged for my review

slides.title: SECTION 19: SAFE AGENT WORKFLOW
slides.html:
SECTION 19: SAFE AGENT WORKFLOW

The 10-Step Safe Agent Protocol

A bulletproof engineering lifecycle for repository-level AI automation

10 STEPS

Steps 1 to 5: Guarded Inception

1. Inspect repo -> 2. Understand current behavior -> 3. Propose incremental plan -> 4. Review risks -> 5. Human approves scope.

Steps 6 to 10: Disciplined Delivery

6. Surgical implementation -> 7. Run automated tests -> 8. Inspect git diff -> 9. Human code review -> 10. Manual commit when verified.

slides.title: SECTION 19: SAFE AGENT WORKFLOW
slides.html:
SECTION 19: SAFE AGENT WORKFLOW

Git as Your Safety Shield

Feature branches, clean commits, and the sacred rule of unstaged changes

GIT SHIELD

Never Let AI Auto-Commit

Keep all changes unstaged. Inspect `git diff` with your own eyes before anything is staged or committed to source control.

The Branch Sandbox

Always run experimental agent tasks on a dedicated git branch (`feature/ai-experiment`). If the agent derails, discard the branch instantly.

$ git checkout -b feature/ai-refactor # Run AI Agent task here... $ git status # Review modified files... $ git diff # If flawless: stage and commit by hand! # If flawed: git restore . && git clean -fd

slides.title: SECTION 19: SAFE AGENT WORKFLOW
slides.html:
SECTION 19: SAFE AGENT WORKFLOW

Red Lines for AI Agents

Operations that must ALWAYS require explicit human authorization

RED LINES

Critical Infrastructure Hazards

Never allow automated agents to: 1. Run database resets. 2. Push to main. 3. Deploy to production. 4. Change cloud credentials. 5. Alter billing settings.

External Network Calls

Beware of prompt injections in untrusted external inputs. Review any command that fetches external scripts or sends tokens over the network.

Forbidden ActionCatastrophic RiskHuman Safeguard
git push origin mainUntested code liveProtected branches in GitHub
pnpm db:resetComplete data wipeRead-only database roles
curl ... | bashArbitrary code injectionInspect scripts before pipe

slides.title: SECTION 20: THINKING ABOUT TRADEOFFS
slides.html:
SECTION 20: THINKING ABOUT TRADEOFFS

Technical Decisions Have No Free Lunches

Forcing AI to analyze trade-offs instead of peddling one-size-fits-all hype

TRADEOFFS

The Options Analysis Matrix

Command: 'Provide 3 alternative technical options. For each, compare: Performance, complexity, security, maintenance cost, and failure modes.'

Context-Dependent Superiority

SQLite is better for embedded CLI tools; Neon PostgreSQL is better for distributed web apps. The 'best' tech stack depends entirely on requirements.

TRADEOFF PROMPT: "Do not recommend a single library. Compare: 1. Neon PostgreSQL with PgBouncer vs Supabase 2. Drizzle ORM vs Prisma ORM For each, evaluate: cold-start latency, bundle size, schema migrations, and connection pooling in Next.js Serverless."

slides.title: SECTION 20: THINKING ABOUT TRADEOFFS
slides.html:
SECTION 20: THINKING ABOUT TRADEOFFS

Classical Software Dilemmas

Evaluating real engineering trade-offs with AI assistance

DILEMMAS

Monolith vs Microservices & SQL vs NoSQL

Monoliths simplify transactions and deployments; microservices decouple scaling. Relational databases enforce ACID; document stores allow flexible schemas.

Client vs Server Components

Server Components reduce client JS bundle and protect secrets; Client Components provide instant local state interactivity and event listeners.

10 empirical techniques to confirm code correctness independently

PLAYBOOK

Automated & Compiler Checks

1. Official documentation check. 2. Static type checker (tsc). 3. Linter (eslint). 4. Automated unit test suite. 5. Integration tests.

Runtime & Behavioral Checks

6. Browser console errors. 7. Server log output. 8. Network request payloads. 9. Database query telemetry. 10. Git diff inspection.

slides.part: SECTION 21: HOW TO VERIFY AI ANSWERS
slides.title: SECTION 21: HOW TO VERIFY AI ANSWERS
slides.html:
SECTION 21: HOW TO VERIFY AI ANSWERS

Eloquence Is Not Evidence

Overcoming the psychological trap of polished AI rhetoric

CRITICAL SKEPTICISM

The Smooth Talker Trap

An LLM can write beautifully formatted markdown with professional tone while referencing a library function that was deprecated in 2021 or never existed.

Demand Reproducible Proof

Adopt a zero-trust mindset: Every code snippet is guilty of being broken until proven innocent by a passing test runner or successful build.

Professional Mindset: Polite, professional tone is a feature of language modeling, not a guarantee of software correctness. Code only becomes true when it executes.

slides.title: SECTION 22: HANDLING UNCERTAINTY
slides.html:
SECTION 22: HANDLING UNCERTAINTY

Forcing AI to Declare Uncertainty

Preventing confident guesses when data is incomplete or ambiguous

UNCERTAINTY

The 4-Category Epistemic Prompt

Instruct: 'Classify your answer into: 1. Verified Facts. 2. Strong Inferences. 3. Assumptions. 4. Unknowns. State what information is missing.'

Banning Hallucination in the Prompt

'If you are unsure of an API parameter or database column, say "I need to inspect file X" instead of guessing its syntax.'

EPISTEMIC RESPONSE FORMAT: 1. VERIFIED FACTS: Found table 'users' in db/schema.ts line 14. 2. STRONG INFERENCES: Function uses NextAuth because session is checked. 3. ASSUMPTIONS: Assuming Neon PostgreSQL connection pool port is 5432. 4. UNKNOWNS: Redis configuration not found in repository.

slides.title: SECTION 22: HANDLING UNCERTAINTY
slides.html:
SECTION 22: HANDLING UNCERTAINTY

Navigating Evolving Library Ecosystems

Handling breaking version changes and training data cutoffs

VERSIONS

Version Drift Hazards

Next.js 12 vs 13 vs 15 have radically different routing and server action semantics. Always specify exact major versions in your prompt.

Feeding Current Docs

When using bleeding-edge libraries, feed the official release notes or API reference directly into the prompt context to ground the model.

Version Injection Tip: "We are using Next.js 15.1 with React 19. Do NOT use deprecated getServerSideProps or pages router. Use App Router Server Actions exclusively."

slides.title: SECTION 23: COMMON PROMPTING MISTAKES
slides.html:
SECTION 23: COMMON PROMPTING MISTAKES

The 10 Deadly Prompting Sins (Part 1)

Recognizing and correcting destructive communication anti-patterns

ANTI-PATTERNS

Sin 1: Extreme Vagueness

Problem: 'Fix my bug'. Fix: Provide the exact error message, expected outcome, actual outcome, and reproduction steps.

Sin 2: Monolithic Overload

Problem: Asking for 15 features at once. Fix: Decompose into atomic tasks and deliver them incrementally.

slides.title: SECTION 23: COMMON PROMPTING MISTAKES
slides.html:
SECTION 23: COMMON PROMPTING MISTAKES

The 10 Deadly Prompting Sins (Part 2)

Preventing scope creep, missing constraints, and blind faith

ANTI-PATTERNS

Sin 3: Coding Before Analyzing

Problem: Telling AI to rewrite immediately without reading existing files. Fix: Force a read-only architecture analysis first.

Sin 4: Unstated Constraints

Problem: Forgetting to state 'do not break backward compatibility'. Fix: Include explicit negative boundaries in every prompt.

slides.title: SECTION 23: COMMON PROMPTING MISTAKES
slides.html:
SECTION 23: COMMON PROMPTING MISTAKES

The 10 Deadly Prompting Sins (Part 3)

Fixing symptom-chasing and runaway file churn

ANTI-PATTERNS

Sin 5: Patching Symptoms in a Loop

Problem: Pasting new errors repeatedly without stepping back to understand why the architecture is failing. Fix: Restart with first principles.

Sin 6: Blind Acceptance

Problem: Copy-pasting AI code without testing. Fix: Run the test suite and inspect git diff before committing.

slides.title: SECTION 24: PROMPT ITERATION
slides.html:
SECTION 24: PROMPT ITERATION

The Prompt Refinement Loop

Iterative precision: Honing answers across sequential turns

REFINEMENT

Dialogue as Calibration

Prompting is rarely a single-shot transaction. Use the first response to identify missing context, tighten constraints, and request surgical revisions.

Refinement vs Length

Iteration should add high-signal clarification—not merely make the prompt longer. Clarify ambiguities and remove unproductive tangents.

slides.title: SECTION 24: PROMPT ITERATION
slides.html:
SECTION 24: PROMPT ITERATION

A 3-Step Iteration Walkthrough

Transforming a mediocre draft into a rock-solid production module

WALKTHROUGH

Turn 1 to Turn 2

Turn 1: Initial query returns generic code. Turn 2: 'Good structure, but replace mock array with Drizzle ORM query matching schema in db/schema.ts.'

Turn 2 to Turn 3

Turn 3: 'Now add Zod input validation, wrap in a database transaction, handle unique constraint collision, and add a unit test.'

Turn 1: "Write a function to create a task." → Returns dummy in-memory array. Turn 2: "Connect to our Neon PostgreSQL Drizzle instance in db/client.ts." → Real SQL. Turn 3: "Add Zod validation, check session user_id, handle database error." → Production ready!

Exact prompts for each phase of the project lifecycle

slides.title: SECTION 26: PRACTICAL PROMPT LIBRARY
slides.html:
SECTION 26: PRACTICAL PROMPT LIBRARY

Production-Grade Reusable Prompt Templates

Battle-tested templates with copy-to-clipboard functionality

LIBRARY

1. Codebase Architecture Audit

Do not write or modify code yet. Inspect the existing codebase and explain: 1. Architecture, routing, and file responsibilities. 2. Current feature mechanics & data flow. 3. Dependencies and integrations. 4. Edge-case bugs, security risks, and assumptions. Support findings with file paths.

2. Surgical Bug Investigation

Analyze this error before proposing a fix. Expected: [Describe expected outcome] Observed: [Describe actual outcome] Logs: [Paste first fatal error and stack trace] Task: Identify root cause, explain why it happened, and propose smallest safe fix with a regression test.

3. Read-Only Security Review

Perform a strictly read-only security audit. Audit: Auth guards, SQL injection, IDOR, secret leaks, and multi-tenant isolation. Report findings by Severity (Critical/High/Med) with file paths, line numbers, exploit scenarios, and patches.

4. Database Migration Safety Audit

Analyze this schema change against Neon PostgreSQL. Check for table locks, downtime on large tables, foreign key cascades, and data loss risks. Provide reversible UP and DOWN SQL migrations and verification SELECT queries.

Interactive Scenario & Troubleshooting Exercises

Test your engineering intuition on real-world production incidents

Incident: The application became slow after a release.

Users report that the main dashboard takes 6+ seconds to load. CPU on the database spiked to 98%. What is your FIRST and BEST action?

Incident: Users receive HTTP 403 when updating tasks.

Authentication succeeds, but saving tasks returns status 403 Forbidden. What should you investigate?

During peak traffic, serverless lambdas exhaust PostgreSQL connection slots. What is the correct fix?

Incident: Mobile screen scrolls horizontally (horizontal overflow).

Incident: Vercel build fails with 'Type error: Property does not exist'.

slides.title: SECTION 29: FINAL CHEAT SHEET
slides.html:
SECTION 29: FINAL CHEAT SHEET

The Master Engineering Workflow & Architecture

Understand -> Analyze -> Plan -> Implement -> Test -> Review -> Verify -> Deliver

CHEAT SHEET

The Golden Commandments

1. Define the goal. 2. Provide relevant context. 3. Set strict constraints. 4. Analyze before coding. 5. Test assumptions. 6. Inspect diffs. 7. Verify with evidence.

The Complete Lifecycle

Human Architect defines problem -> AI acts as accelerated copilot -> Human inspects proposals -> Automated suite verifies truth -> Production releases safely.

final-architecture — human & ai symbiosis
Human Developer (Problem Definition & Acceptance Constraints) ↓ AI Copilot / Agent (Read-Only Codebase Analysis & Plan Proposal) ↓ Human Review (Approve Architecture & Validate Assumptions) ↓ AI Implementation (Surgical Unstaged Code Edits) ↓ Automated Verification (tsc, eslint, vitest, EXPLAIN ANALYZE) ↓ Human Verification (git diff, manual test, staging check) ↓ Safe Production Deployment
